t: Wagadou, the Soninke kingdom Arab writers called Ghana, sat between West Africa's goldfields and the Saharan caravan routes.
It grew rich by taxing gold going north and salt going south, and its gold supplied mints across North Africa and Muslim Spain.
Almoravid attacks, shifting trade routes and drought broke its power; Mali absorbed what remained in the thirteenth century.
dyk: Ghana's king kept every gold nugget found in the kingdom for himself, letting subjects trade only gold dust, a deliberate way to stop the price of gold from collapsing.
ev: Wagadou crystallises as a recognisable state under Soninke rule
Ghana captures Awdaghast, the southern terminus of the western trans-Saharan route
The Almoravids seize Awdaghast, ending some sixty years of Ghanaian control
Al-Bakri completes his famous description of the gilded royal court
Almoravids sack Koumbi Saleh, reducing Ghana for a time to a tributary
Death of the Almoravid leader Abu Bakr ibn Umar lets the Soninke regain independence
Sundiata Keita defeats Sumanguru at Kirina; Ghana's remnant passes into the Mali Empire
The old capital is traditionally said to have been abandoned
